lead: A smart city puts many small sensing deployments under one city authority: traffic, street lights, waste bins, water lines and parking. Each deployment is small. The value comes from sharing one network, one cloud and one dashboard. Smart parking is the clearest complete example. A sensor in each bay reports whether a car is there, a low-power wide-area network carries that one piece of news, a cloud service keeps the slot map, and a driver app sells the slot and takes payment. This chapter follows that chain and shows how to pick the radio link for each part.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 on LPWAN, NB-IoT and MQTT, and Unit 5 on IoT cloud services.

sections.h3: What a smart city actually deploys

blocks.text: A smart city uses sensors, networks and data to run city services with fewer manual checks and less waste. It is not one system. It is a portfolio of small deployments under one authority, sharing a network and a cloud platform.

items: Mobility. Inductive loops and radar counters at junctions count vehicles; the count feeds signal timing. Bus position comes from a GPS unit on the bus. Number-plate cameras need a high data rate and are a separate, wired or 4G service.
Street lighting. A photocell and a motion sensor per pole dim the lamp when the road is empty. The saving appears on the electricity bill, which is why this is often the first project funded.
Waste. An ultrasonic sensor in each bin reports fill level, so trucks collect only the bins that are full.
Water. Flow and pressure sensors at valves find leaks and measure supply; see 6.5 for the water chain in detail.

blocks.text: The shared part matters in exams. One low-power wide-area network can carry parking, bins and meters together. One cloud platform holds the dashboards, billing and alarms. Adding a service then means adding devices and a message topic, not building a new network.

sections.h3: Smart parking: from slot sensor to payment

blocks.text: Sensing. An in-ground sensor is a magnetometer buried in the bay. A car changes the local magnetic field by a few microtesla, and the node reports occupied or free. It needs no wiring and lasts years on one battery, but the road must be opened to replace it. An overhead sensor, ultrasonic or camera on a pole, is easy to service but needs power and a cable.
Message. The sensor sends a state change, plus a heartbeat every 5 minutes, about 60 bytes. It is not a video and not a continuous stream.

Radio. NB-IoT fits this job. A 180 kHz carrier gives tens of kbit/s uplink, far more than 60 bytes needs. The link budget is roughly 20 dB better than GSM, so a sensor under a car in a basement still reaches the cell. Power saving mode and extended discontinuous reception let the modem sleep for minutes, with the network holding any message. The price is latency of seconds to tens of seconds.

Deployment. In a baseline deployment the operator adds an NB-IoT carrier to base stations it already owns, in-band or guard-band with LTE, or standalone in refarmed GSM spectrum, and upgrades the core for cellular IoT. The city buys SIMs and an access point name; it does not buy base stations. Because you cannot dig up 5000 sensors to test them, coverage and capacity are first simulated with system-level or ray-tracing tools, then checked with a pilot of a few hundred sensors.

Path. The sensor publishes to a topic such as parking/slot/17 with a retained payload, and the cloud subscribes over MQTT. The cloud updates the slot map and offers it to the driver app, which reserves, takes a UPI payment, and holds the slot for a short time. The barrier opens on the number plate or a QR code; its camera sits on 4G or Ethernet, never on NB-IoT.

sections.h3: Choosing the link for each part of the vehicle system

blocks.text: One car park uses several links at once. Pick the slowest link that carries the required data rate, then check power and cost.

The rule is simple. A slot sensor needs 320 bit/s and must run for years, so NB-IoT wins on power and cost. The barrier camera needs megabits for live video, so 4G or Ethernet wins on rate, and mains power is available anyway. The gate controller answers in milliseconds, so a wired or Wi-Fi link wins on latency. A vehicle telematics unit that streams location uses 4G because it is already powered from the car.

figure.caption: A slot sensor sends one small NB-IoT message every 5 minutes through the operator core to the parking cloud, which updates the slot and bills the driver's app. Notice that the message is bytes, not video.

spec.title: Smart parking message path
spec.aria: A parking slot sensor sends 60-byte messages every 5 minutes through the NB-IoT base station and operator core to a parking cloud, which sends the slot state and bill to a driver app.

examples.question: A car park has 200 slots. Each slot sensor sends one 60-byte message every 5 minutes. Find the average uplink bit rate and the data volume per day.
steps: Messages per slot per hour = 60 min ÷ 5 min = 12.
Total messages per hour = 200 slots × 12 = 2400 messages/hour.
Convert to per second: 2400 ÷ 3600 s = 0.6667 messages/s.
Bits per message = 60 B × 8 bit/B = 480 bit.
Average uplink rate = 0.6667 messages/s × 480 bit = 320 bit/s.
Check: 320 bit/s × 86,400 s ÷ 8 = 3,456,000 B, which agrees.
examples.answer: The average uplink rate is 320 bit/s, and the park sends 3.456 MB per day (about 0.6667 messages per second).
examples.check:
slots = 200
msg_bytes = 60
period_min = 5
per_slot_hour = 60 / period_min
total_hour = slots * per_slot_hour
per_second = total_hour / 3600
rate_bps = per_second * msg_bytes * 8
daily_messages = total_hour * 24
daily_bytes = daily_messages * msg_bytes
daily_mb = daily_bytes / 1e6
print(round(per_second, 4))
print(round(rate_bps, 2))
print(round(daily_mb, 3))

traps: NB-IoT is for small, infrequent uplink. Do not put the barrier camera's live video on it; that camera needs 4G or Ethernet.
Convert messages per hour to messages per second by dividing by 3600 before finding a bit rate. Forgetting the 3600 gives an answer 3600 times too large.
Bytes and bits are different. A 60-byte message is 480 bits; state your unit at every step.
NB-IoT latency is seconds, so the barrier cannot wait for the cloud to open the gate. The gate controller decides locally and reports afterwards.
A smart city is not one giant sensor network. It is many deployments sharing a platform, and each has its own data rate and power budget.

quiz.q: What physical quantity does an in-ground parking slot sensor measure?
quiz.a: The local magnetic field. The metal mass of a car changes it by a few microtesla, which the magnetometer reads as occupied.

quiz.q: Why is NB-IoT preferred over Wi-Fi for in-ground slot sensors?
quiz.a: The sensor is buried, so it needs deep indoor and underground penetration, and the link budget of NB-IoT is about 20 dB better than GSM. It runs for years on one cell using power saving mode. It sends tiny payloads, which matches its tens of kbit/s uplink. No site cabling or access point is needed; the operator owns the network.

quiz.q: A car park has 500 slots. Each sensor sends a 40-byte message every 10 minutes. Find the average uplink bit rate and the daily data volume.
quiz.a: Messages per slot per hour = 6. Total per hour = 500 × 6 = 3000. Per second = 3000 ÷ 3600 = 0.8333. Bits per message = 40 × 8 = 320 bit. Rate = 0.8333 × 320 = 266.7 bit/s. Daily messages = 3000 × 24 = 72,000. Daily volume = 72,000 × 40 B = 2,880,000 B = 2.88 MB.

quiz.q: A designer must connect a slot sensor, a barrier number-plate camera and a gate controller inside one car park. Choose a link for each and justify it in one line.
quiz.a: Slot sensor: NB-IoT, because the rate needed is a few hundred bit/s and the device must last years on a battery. Camera: 4G or Ethernet, because live video needs megabits and mains power is available. Gate controller: wired or Wi-Fi, because opening the barrier needs millisecond response on site.

quiz.q: What is the role of MQTT in the parking system?
quiz.a: MQTT is the publish-subscribe message path. The sensor or its gateway publishes to a topic such as parking/slot/17 with a retained state, and the parking cloud subscribes. The two sides do not need to know each other's address, and the retained message gives a new subscriber the latest state immediately.

quiz.q: A vendor proposes sending one frame of video from every slot every 5 minutes over NB-IoT instead of a 60-byte status message. Analyse the proposal.
quiz.a: A compressed frame is tens of kB, roughly a thousand times the 60-byte message, so the uplink rate and the daily volume rise by that factor and the data plan cost follows. NB-IoT uplink is tens of kbit/s, so each frame takes many seconds, and latency already runs to seconds. Radio-on time per message grows, so the multi-year battery life collapses and buried sensors must be dug up and replaced. The correct design is a cheap sensor on NB-IoT, with a camera on 4G doing local processing only where an image is genuinely needed.

quiz.q: Why are NB-IoT networks simulated before a city-wide parking rollout?
quiz.a: You cannot install thousands of buried sensors to test coverage. Simulation with system-level or ray-tracing tools predicts path loss in basements and street canyons, estimates how many sensors one cell carries, and shows where repeaters or extra carriers are needed. It turns a rollout into a design problem, and a small pilot then confirms the prediction.

quiz.q: Name three smart city services other than parking that use the same shared network.
quiz.a: Any three of: street lighting control, waste-bin fill level, water flow and leak monitoring, vehicle counting at junctions, bus tracking, electricity metering.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real city platforms increasingly separate the device layer from the service layer, so a parking operator can rent connectivity and cloud from the city instead of building both. Standards work on NB-IoT keeps adding features such as small-packet transmission and non-IP data delivery, which matter when thousands of devices send a few bytes each. Research looks at joint sensing and communication, where the same radio echo that carries data also detects the car. Search next for NB-IoT coverage planning, MQTT retained messages, and open parking data standards.
